output.label: Low back or hip

output.label: Shoulder

output.label: Triathlon
output.blurb: Swim, bike and run — the plan covers all three plus the durability they demand

output.label: Sprint
output.blurb: 750m / 20k / 5k — strength and power transfer strongly

profile.rationale: Sprint distance is short and hard, so maximal strength and rate of force development transfer directly. Main lifts stay heavy at 4–6 reps and the power session earns its place.

output.label: Olympic
output.blurb: 1.5k / 40k / 10k — moderate volume, real room for strength work

profile.rationale: Olympic distance still rewards heavy strength work, and your weekly sport hours leave room for it. Main lifts run at 4–6 reps.

output.label: Half (70.3)
output.blurb: 1.9k / 90k / 21k — lifting shifts toward durability

profile.rationale: At half distance your legs are already absorbing a lot of eccentric load, so the plyometrics come out and the lifting shifts toward durability — calves and hip stability first, at 5–8 reps.

output.label: Full (140.6)
output.blurb: 3.8k / 180k / 42k — minimum effective dose only

profile.rationale: Full distance means the training itself is the limiter. Lifting drops to a minimum effective dose at 6–8 reps, aimed squarely at the tissues that break down over an Ironman — calves, hamstrings and hip stabilisers.

output.label: 5k

output.label: 10k
output.blurb: Strength and economy, with slightly more mileage to respect

profile.rationale: 10k still rewards maximal strength and elastic return, so the heavy work and the power session both stay. Volume comes down a touch to respect the extra mileage.

output.label: Half marathon
output.blurb: Economy plus durability — the tissues need to last

profile.rationale: Half-marathon training piles up eccentric load, so the jumping comes out and heavy-slow calf, hamstring and hip-abduction work comes in. Main lifts run at 5–8 reps.

output.splitReason: One session a week holds the strength you have. It won't build much, which is the right trade at this point in your season.

slots.why: Peak hip and knee extension force — the strength that shows up as sustainable power on the bike and a cheaper stride on the run.
Posterior-chain strength is the best-supported protective factor for the run leg, and it powers the top of the pedal stroke.
Bent-knee calf work loads the soleus — the largest force contributor in running gait, and the tissue most often under-prepared for it. Three seconds down on every rep.
Anti-rotation strength holds the aero position without leaking power, and keeps your pelvis honest as the run wears on.

rationale: Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
Sprint: Sprint distance is short and hard, so maximal strength and rate of force development transfer directly. Main lifts stay heavy at 4–6 reps and the power session earns its place.

Bent-knee calf work loads the soleus — the largest force contributor in running gait, and the tissue most often under-prepared for it. Three seconds down on every rep.
Anti-rotation strength holds the aero position without leaking power, and keeps your pelvis honest as the run wears on.
Loaded single-leg hip extension is the closest the gym gets to a pedal stroke, and it exposes the side-to-side asymmetry bilateral lifting hides.
Vertical pulling strength for the catch — the phase of the stroke where propulsion is actually generated.

budget.warning: You asked for 4 lifting days, but at 12+ hours of triathlon a week the plan uses 2. Lifting that costs you a quality session in your sport is a net loss — the extra day is better spent recovering.

rationale: Two or three sessions a week of heavy, low-volume, multi-joint lifting is the dose the concurrent-training research supports for endurance athletes — enough to raise maximal strength, cheap enough that your sport keeps its recovery.
Every main lift stops two to three reps short of failure. The strength adaptation does not need the last rep; your next session does need the recovery it would cost.
Volume sits well under a bodybuilding dose on purpose: added muscle mass is weight you carry for the whole race, and rising tonnage is a cost here rather than a sign of progress.
